seo.title: Karmic tail 18 9 18 compatibility: two Moons and the Hermit
seo.description: Karmic tail 18 9 18 compatibility: the Moon at the entry, the Hermit in the middle, the Moon again as the main task — read through Cyrano de Bergerac.

title: The 18-9-18 karmic tail in compatibility: a couple who recognise each other in the dark
short: The Moon, the Hermit and the Moon again: the 18-9-18 tail begins at night and ends at night, with a long silence between the two nights. Nobody has this tail in a personal chart; it appears only in the sum of two charts. It belongs to a couple who understand each other best in half-light — in letters and messages, in hints, in talk after midnight — and who keep quiet about the main thing in daylight longer than anyone else.

sections.h2: A tail that belongs to no one
paragraphs: Every point of a couple's matrix is the sum of the matching points of two personal matrices, reduced to 22. A couple's tail is read in the order M–N–D: entry to the task, middle of the task, main task. The 18-9-18 tail has an oddity, and the investigation starts there: it never occurs as a personal tail. In a personal matrix the entry M equals the main task D plus the centre of the chart, and with D = 18 no centre can give an entry of 18. So neither partner brings this tail into the relationship. It arises only between the two of them.

It occurs in roughly one couple in 104 (0.963%), 38th of the 97 couple tails. And it is almost always assembled from two particular personal tails: 12-19-7 in one partner and 6-17-11 in the other (85% of such couples), or 12-16-4 and 6-20-14 (15%). A third route, two identical 9-18-9 tails, is arithmetically possible but so rare that it rounds to zero.
Break the couple's points down into their sums and the first clues appear:

ul: **Entry:** the Moon is made of one partner's Hanged Man and the other's Lovers, 12 + 6. The entry almost never has any other components.
**Middle:** the Hermit is born of the Sun and the Star (19 + 17 = 36 → 9) or of the Tower and Judgement (16 + 20 = 36 → 9). Two lights of the sky, the Sun and the Star, add up to a single lantern.
**Main task:** the Moon is made of the Chariot and Strength (7 + 11) or of the Emperor and Temperance (4 + 14). Two cards of will and self-command together give the card of fog.

paragraphs: Rostand wrote lines that sound like a description of this arithmetic. Cyrano offers the handsome Christian an alliance: one will supply the words, the other the face. "Will you complete me, and let me complete you?" he asks, in the 1898 translation by Gladys Thomas and Mary F. Guillemard quoted here throughout; and then, more briefly: "Let me be wit for you, be you my beauty!" Roxane will fall in love with a man who does not exist on his own. He exists only as the sum of two.

The 18-9-18 tail works the same way, but this is not a story about a love triangle: in a real couple there is no third person. "Christian" here is the pleasant version of oneself that is fit for daylight, the one each partner pushes forward while the real voice speaks from the shadow.

sections.h2: Act III: the whole tail in one night
paragraphs: Act III is called "Roxane's Kiss". It lasts one night on a small square in old Paris, and its three main scenes come in exactly the order of the tail's cards.

**The Moon.** Christian cannot talk to Roxane, so Cyrano stands under her balcony, in the dark: first he prompts, then he speaks himself. He refuses to climb into the light and explains why — it is "the rare occasion, when our hearts can speak / Our selves unseen, unseeing!" And at once he gives the formula of the whole couple: "I but a shadow--you a radiance fair!"

**The Hermit.** In the middle of the declaration a Capuchin friar appears on the square. Rostand's stage direction: he enters "with a lantern. He goes from house to house, looking at every door." Cyrano greets him with a joke: "What do you, playing at Diogenes?" Diogenes, as Diogenes Laërtius tells it, walked about in broad daylight with a lit lamp, saying he was looking for a man. The friar is looking for Roxane's house and carries a letter for her; Cyrano sends him the wrong way, and he comes back when the kiss has already happened. Once the wedding is settled, the friar turns his lantern on Cyrano — "'Tis you?" — and only after Christian answers "'Tis I!" does he move the light to the handsome face. The lantern finds first the man Roxane has really fallen in love with that night: this is our reading, but the words and stage directions are Rostand's. The wedding itself takes place inside the house, with no audience, and it will be announced after the fact.

**The Moon again.** To keep de Guiche from going in and stopping the wedding, Cyrano pulls his hat down over his eyes, changes his voice and drops from the balcony on a branch, as if he had crashed from the sky: "Like a bomb / I fell from the moon!" While the wedding goes on inside, he lists the ways of rising to the Moon and names the tide as the seventh: "I' th' witching hour when the moon woos the wave". Then he speaks in his own voice: "The quarter's gone--I'll hinder you no more: / The marriage-vows are made." Footmen bring out candelabra, Cyrano takes off his hat — and in the light he is known by his voice and by his nose.

The same scene holds a detail that will return at the end. Roxane first reads de Guiche's letter to herself by lantern light, and aloud she reads something else entirely: that the Cardinal orders her to marry Christian at once. "Am I not apt at reading letters?" she whispers to the bridegroom. **The union begins with a letter read falsely.** Fifteen years later there will be another letter and another reading.

sections.h2: Entry to the task — the Moon: talking without seeing each other
paragraphs: The entry to the task shows what the couple wants together: shared wishes, agreements, that very "common language". In the compatibility reading this point carries a second label too — "Common language". For 18-9-18 the common language is lunar. The two are happiest where neither has to show themselves completely: in long correspondence, in voice messages after midnight, in jokes only they understand, in things left unsaid that stir more than a plain word.

Cyrano explains why night makes it easier: "In the tender, sheltering dusk / I dare to be myself for once,--at last!" This is the paradox of the lunar entry. Darkness hides the face and frees the voice. A person in such a couple often says the truest things where they cannot be seen: they write what they would never say at the table, and at the table they joke about what they wrote in earnest at night.

Roxane hears the difference at once — "'Tis true, your voice rings with a tone that's new" — and asks nothing. She likes the mystery, and the mystery suits her. This is the other side of point M: it stands on the line of tasks, and what the two want can become their resistance. A wish for mystery easily turns into an unspoken agreement not to ask awkward questions.

This is how an image, rather than a portrait, forms at the start of the union. Each partner fills the other in by reflected light — from letters, from a couple of phrases, from their own hopes. Already in Act I Cyrano tells a friend how it goes. On a spring evening, in a garden, he watches a knight with a lady on his arm and dreams for a moment "To saunter thus 'neath the moonshine" — and then: "--The shadow of my profile on the wall!" The same moon gives him both the dream and the shadow of his nose. That is how the lunar entry works: the half-light that makes a meeting magical also draws the fear of looking ridiculous.

Later Christian speaks for everyone who has to live beside such an image: "Too long I've borne about within myself / A rival to myself". For a couple with this tail the rival is usually not a person. More often it is that first version of oneself — from the letters, from the start of the romance — that one has to compete with for years.

sections.h2: Middle of the task — the Hermit: fifteen years of Saturdays
paragraphs: Act V is called "Cyrano's Gazette". Fifteen years have passed: 1655, autumn, the park of the Sisters of the Holy Cross in Paris. The stage direction puts "an enormous plane tree in the middle of the stage, standing alone". Roxane lives here as a widow, in a black veil, and wears Christian's last letter on her breast. Cyrano comes every Saturday at the same hour. Roxane says of him: "I hear,--for now I never turn to look-- / Too sure to hear his cane tap down the steps".

The middle of the task is how the couple lives the path from the shared wish to the main task. The Hermit in the middle is loyalty and silence at once. The plus here is real: not a single Saturday missed, the chair in the shade, the embroidery he teases with the same joke every time, love shown in deeds rather than words. The minus is just as real: each of them sits under this tree with a wound and keeps it hidden.

Cyrano recites to Roxane her "gazette", the news of the week. The King overate on fruit preserve and was bled; hundreds of candles burned at the Queen's ball; Madame d'Athis's little dog had to take a dose. News of everyone — and not a word about himself. To the nuns he boasts, "Sister, I eat meat on Friday!", while the Mother Superior knows that the last time he came he had not eaten for two days. No one can help him: "He permits not."

On the last Saturday he arrives wounded, his hat pulled down over his eyes, and explains his faint by an old wound from Arras. Roxane answers, "Each of us has his wound; ay, I have mine,-- / Never healed up", and puts her hand on her breast, where the letter hangs. Both speak of wounds. He passes off a fresh wound as an old one. She shows her old one and does not know that the author of the letter under which she aches is sitting in the next chair.

In a modern couple this Hermit looks ordinary. There is a ritual — Sunday dinner, an evening walk, a call at the same time every day — and it holds the union together for years. Inside the ritual they discuss colleagues, relatives, TV series, prices. About "I'm scared", "I'm tired", "I miss you" they keep quiet: sometimes out of care, so as not to worry the other, sometimes out of pride, so as not to look weak. Each withdraws into a shell exactly when things are hard, though the Hermit's task in a couple is the opposite: not to hide at a hard moment, but to share and to help.

This act holds an exchange that reads like a caption to the card. De Guiche, having heard dangerous rumours, asks Le Bret to warn his friend: "Let him stay in--be prudent!" Le Bret raises his arms to heaven: "Prudent! He!..." Cyrano, who all his life has thrown himself alone against a hundred swords, is the least prudent man in the play. And the most cautious in love: for fifteen years he guards a single sentence. Even news about himself he will deliver the Hermit's way: after the fact, in the third person, as the last line of his "gazette".

sections.h2: Main task — the Moon: "How can you read? It is too dark to see!"
paragraphs: A couple's main task is read mainly through its minus: what the two cannot manage and what they have to learn. For 18-9-18 this is the Moon again, the same card as at the entry. But in the finale of the play it works the other way round.

Cyrano asks to read the very letter of Christian's that he once wrote himself. The stage directions follow one another: "Twilight begins to fall." "The shades of evening fall imperceptibly." "The darkness deepens." He reads aloud, and Roxane is no longer listening to the words but to the voice: "It is not the first time I hear that voice!" She quietly steps behind the chair, looks at the letter and puts her hand on his shoulder: "How can you read? It is too dark to see!"

In the original the two night scenes share the same words. Under the balcony Cyrano excuses his faltering: "C'est qu'il fait nuit" — "it is because it is night". In the convent garden Roxane says: "Il fait nuit" — "it is night". **The same night that hid him at the start gave him away at the end.** This is the meaning of one card at both ends of the tail. The couple does not need to escape the Moon. It needs the darkness to stop being a shelter for the image and to become the place where people are recognised by their voice.

Rostand shows the minus of the main task without mercy. The image built at the start collapses, and Roxane loses one man twice: "I loved but once, yet twice I lose my love!" Cyrano denies everything to the last, and the denial gives him away by itself: "No, my sweet love, I never loved you!" The lie is spoken, but "my sweet love" already tells the truth.

There is also a piece of evidence he had forbidden himself. In Act I Cyrano will not let himself weep: "Think, how vilely suited / Adown this nose a tear its passage tracing!" Tenderness seems ridiculous to him, and he hides it. But on the farewell letter he composed for Christian, his tear remained — "A tear!", Christian noticed at the time. In the finale it is this tear that settles the matter: "The tears were your tears?" — "The bloodstains were his." **What he hid as weakness turned out to be the only proof of his love.**

Benebell Wen, discussing the reversed Moon, writes: "The repressed latent will always surface, and any strong intention to repress will cause a violent surfacing." The harder something is held down, the more sharply it breaks out. Rostand lets fifteen years of silence break out in a few minutes of dusk. And Roxane asks the question that an 18-9-18 couple can ask itself before it gets dark: "Why, why keep silence".

The bitterest line in the scene is hers: "I should have guessed, each time he said my name!" She heard the other voice already under the balcony. The knowledge was with her for all fifteen years; what was missing was the question.

sections.h2: Two Moons: each lights the other with reflected light
paragraphs: Rostand's hero had a model: Savinien de Cyrano de Bergerac (1619–1655), poet and freethinker. Twenty months after his death his friend Henry Le Bret published his fantastic novel about a journey to the Moon, the Comical History of the States and Empires of the Moon (1657); today it is often known as The Other World. The novel opens with an argument on a night road: a full moon, friends guessing what it might be, and the narrator saying: "I believe that the Moon is a world like this one, to which ours serves as a moon" (our translation).

For a couple with two Moons in its tail there is no better formula. Each sees the other as a moon: by reflected light, in whatever phase their own hopes and fears allow them to make out. And each forgets that to the other they are a moon too — shining not with their own light but with what the other puts into them.

Rostand knew the book. His Cyrano calls the Moon "that saffron-colored ball", and the real Cyrano, on the first page of his novel, a "boule de safran", a saffron ball. And the first of the seven ways of reaching the Moon with which Cyrano bamboozles de Guiche — rising with dew that the sun draws upwards — is the very way the novel's hero flies off. In the finale of the play the Moon and Roxane stand side by side. Cyrano tells Roxane: "I owe it to you that I had at least one woman friend" (our translation; Thomas and Guillemard have "But I have had your friendship"). Le Bret points to the moonlight between the branches: "Your other friend is here, come to see you" (our translation). In Thomas and Guillemard's version the line is "Your other lady-love is come." Two friends, and both are Moons. One of them he saw all his life from below, from afar, by reflected light. And to her he was a voice from the dark.

The real story around the play is lunar too. Roxane's model was Cyrano's cousin on his mother's side, Madeleine Robineau, Baroness de Neuvillette. Her husband, Baron Christophe de Neuvillette, died at the siege of Arras in 1640. Widowed, she gave up worldly life and turned to devotion. Mother Marguerite of Act V is real as well: Marguerite de Senaux, in religion Marguerite de Jésus, was prioress of the Daughters of the Cross, the convent that Cyrano's sister Catherine entered in 1641. And the anecdote collection Menagiana preserved a detail about the real Cyrano that might have come straight from the Moon card: because of his disfigured nose he could not bear to be looked at.

sections.h2: Waite and Wen: a Capuchin with a lantern and a generous deception
paragraphs: Arthur Edward Waite, in The Pictorial Key to the Tarot, lists the old names of the Hermit. In common parlance, he writes, "he is also the Capuchin, and in more philosophical language the Sage." By placing a Capuchin friar with a lantern between the two moon scenes, Rostand repeats the card's old name literally. Wen, too, links the Hermit with friars of a mendicant order — the Hermits of Saint Francis of Paola, "later known as the Minim Friars".

Waite's divinatory meanings for the Hermit begin with "Prudence, circumspection". For the reversed card he gives "Concealment, disguise, policy, fear, unreasoned caution". It is almost an exact portrait of Cyrano in love — a man whom Le Bret cannot even imagine being prudent.

In Waite's divinatory list the Moon has "deception", and the reversed card "lesser degrees of deception and error". In the original, Roxane calls the whole story "la généreuse imposture", a generous imposture ("the generous counterfeit" in Thomas and Guillemard). The lunar deception in this couple is not about gain or malice. It is the deception of shame: a person hides not to take something that belongs to someone else, but because they do not believe their real self will be accepted. The card does not prove that anyone in the couple is lying: it shows where the two can easily mistake each other.
Two dates from the same year and even the same day of the month, four months apart. The partners' personal tails:
Now add up the matching points:

The couple's middle is the sum of the two personal middles; it is not recalculated from the couple's outer numbers. The couple's centre, the atmosphere inside the union, is the Moon here too: so it is in 91.1% of couples with this tail, while the other 8.9% have the Hermit in the centre. The couple's values in the example are 9, the Hermit: so it is in 71.5% of such couples, and 28.5% have the Moon. One more Moon stands in the point "What to create together", which is made from the birth months (7 + 11 = 18). The tail's two cards spread across the whole matrix: night and lantern are not an episode here but the climate.

The play ends in darkness, but the numbers predict neither its ending nor any other. The tail shows a plot, not a fate, and it can be lived differently. Rostand himself left hints for an 18-9-18 couple — at the places where the plot could have turned.

ul: **Believe the permission already given.** In Act IV Roxane tells Cyrano she would love Christian ugly — "Yes, ugly!" — and to "Disfigured" she answers "Ay!". Cyrano believes it for a moment — "My God! it's true, perchance, love waits me there!" — and does not get to finish. In an 18-9-18 couple the permission to be oneself has often already been given. The task is to take it seriously.

**Ask instead of filling in.** Roxane hears "a tone that's new" and asks no question. The Moon in the main task asks for guesses to be checked with words — "what did you mean?" — rather than with one's own version of the answer, and for one's fears not to be loaded onto the partner.

**Say in daylight what is easy to write at night.** Letters and night conversations are this couple's native language, and there is no need to give them up. But one sentence said aloud, face to face, weighs more than a dozen letters.

**Add a line about oneself to the "gazette".** The Hermit's ritual is the couple's strength, and it does not have to be invented. It has room for one piece of news that is not about the world but about oneself: "I'm tired", "I'm scared", "I'm happy with you".

**Tell solitude from disappearance.** The Hermit needs time of his own, and withdrawing into oneself is a way to restore strength, not a lack of love. But it is said aloud: "I need some time alone" is not at all the same as a silence fifteen years long.

sections.h2: The strong version of the tail
paragraphs: In the plus, both cards give the two a rare gift. The Moon gives intuition: Roxane recognised the voice in the dark, by its tone, after fifteen years. The Moon also gives imagination and play, a shared secret world in which the partner keeps surprising the other years later. The Hermit gives a loyalty that needs no witnesses, the ability to be together without unnecessary words, a friendship that lasts for decades.

A strong 18-9-18 couple keeps its night language and adds a daytime one. It can still talk for hours in the dark — but it no longer hides there. Its "il fait nuit" means only one thing: time to light the lamp and finish the conversation.

The same numbers make two more couple tails. In 9-18-18 (1.228% of couples, the Moon in the centre for 66.8%) the couple enters through the Hermit — wanting quiet and a corner of its own — and then lives and learns through the Moon. In 18-18-9 (0.221% of couples, the Hermit in the centre for 82%) the couple enters and lives through the Moon, and the Hermit becomes the main task: learning a solitude that does not drive the two apart. In 18-9-18 the Moon stands at both ends, and the Hermit's silence becomes a bridge between two nights.

ul: **Entry to the task — The Moon.** What the two want together: mystery, understanding without words, a private language of half-tones. Along with that wish an image enters the union: each shows the other a slightly polished version of themselves.
**Middle of the task — The Hermit.** How the couple lives its path: loyalty, rituals, respect for each other's solitude — and the habit of carrying the hardest things alone.
**Main task — The Moon.** What the couple has to learn: to tell the living person from the image formed at the start, and to speak about feelings in daylight instead of waiting for dark.

intro: This story has already been written. In Edmond Rostand's Cyrano de Bergerac (first performed on 28 December 1897) the whole romance rests on a voice from the dark, and the 18-9-18 tail is played out in it twice: within a single night in Act III, and across the fifteen years between the balcony and the convent garden. What follows is an investigation: the clues in the numbers, in the text of the play and in the books about the cards.

faq.q: What does the 18-9-18 karmic tail mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a couple's tail in which the entry to the task and the main task are the Moon and the middle is the Hermit. The two are drawn together by a language of mystery and half-tones, they walk their path in loyalty and silence, and what they have to learn is to tell the living person from the image and to speak about feelings directly, in daylight.

faq.q: Can 18-9-18 be the karmic tail of a personal destiny matrix?
faq.a: No. In a personal matrix the entry of the tail equals the main task plus the centre of the chart, and with a main task of 18 no centre gives an entry of 18. Anyone who sees the triple 18-9-18 is looking at a couple's matrix: this tail exists only in compatibility.

faq.q: How is the 18-9-18 couple tail calculated?
faq.a: Add up the matching points of the two personal tails and reduce the sums to 22: entry with entry, middle with middle, main task with main task. For example, 12-19-7 and 6-17-11 give 12 + 6 = 18, 19 + 17 = 36 → 9 and 7 + 11 = 18.

faq.q: Is 18-9-18 a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. The tail shows a couple's tasks, not a verdict, and the method gives no compatibility percentages. The Moon and the Hermit have real strengths — intuition, imagination, loyalty, deep friendship. There is one difficulty, and it can be seen in advance: the habit of hiding the main thing and loving an image instead of a person.

faq.q: How common is the 18-9-18 couple tail?
faq.a: Roughly one couple in 104 (0.963%), 38th of the 97 couple tails. In 85% of cases it is made of the personal tails 12-19-7 and 6-17-11, in 15% of 12-16-4 and 6-20-14.

report: Roxane, in Cyrano de Bergerac, fell in love with a man who did not exist on his own. Cyrano gave him the words; the handsome Christian gave him the face. Cyrano proposes the deal himself: he will be the wit, Christian the beauty. The 18-9-18 tail works the same way: nobody has it in a personal chart, and it appears only in the sum of two charts. It belongs to a couple who understand each other best in half-light — in letters and messages, in hints, in talk after midnight — and who keep quiet about the main thing in daylight longer than anyone else. In a real couple there is no third person: "Christian" here is the version of oneself fit for daylight, the one each partner pushes forward while the real voice speaks from the shadow.

report.h3: The whole tail in one night

report: Act III of the play lasts a single night, and its three scenes come in exactly the order of the cards. First the Moon. Cyrano stands in the dark under Roxane's balcony and refuses to climb into the light; it is "the rare occasion, when our hearts can speak / Our selves unseen, unseeing!" Night makes it easier for him: "I dare to be myself for once,--at last!" Darkness hides the face and frees the voice.

Then the Hermit. A Capuchin friar crosses the square with a lantern in his hand, and Cyrano jokingly calls him Diogenes. Among the Hermit's old names Waite gives this one too: "he is also the Capuchin". The friar is looking for Roxane's house, and once the wedding is settled his lantern falls first on Cyrano — and only then on the bridegroom's handsome face. The wedding itself takes place inside the house, with no audience.

And the Moon again. So that nobody can stop the ceremony, Cyrano pulls his hat over his eyes, changes his voice and drops from the balcony: "Like a bomb / I fell from the moon!" The union begins with a lunar fib — and with a letter that Roxane read aloud falsely.

For this couple the entry to the task is a common language of half-tones. The two are happiest where neither has to show themselves completely: in long correspondence, in voice messages after midnight, in jokes only they understand. Roxane notices that Christian's voice has suddenly changed, and asks nothing. A wish for mystery easily becomes an unspoken agreement not to ask awkward questions.

Act V is a convent garden fifteen years later. Roxane lives there as a widow and wears Christian's last letter on her breast. Cyrano comes every Saturday at the same hour and recites her "gazette": the King overate on fruit preserve, hundreds of candles burned at the ball. News of everyone — and not a word about himself. He boasts to the nuns that he ate meat on Friday, when in fact he has not eaten for two days. On the last Saturday he arrives wounded and passes off a fresh wound as an old one. Roxane answers that each of us has a wound "Never healed up", and puts her hand on the letter, not knowing that its author is sitting in the next chair.

This is the Hermit in the middle: **loyalty and silence at once.** Not a single Saturday missed, love shown in deeds — and each carries the hardest things alone. In a modern couple it is the Sunday dinner or the call at the same time every day, where everything is discussed except "I'm scared" and "I feel lonely". When Le Bret is asked to warn his friend to be prudent, he raises his arms to heaven: "Prudent! He!..." A man who throws himself alone against a hundred swords guards a single sentence for fifteen years. Waite's divinatory meanings for the Hermit begin with "Prudence", and for the reversed card they end with "unreasoned caution".

report.h3: One night hides, another gives away

report: The main task is the Moon again, but in the finale it works the other way round. Cyrano asks to read Christian's letter — the one he once wrote himself. The stage directions follow in turn: "Twilight begins to fall." "The shades of evening fall imperceptibly." "The darkness deepens." Roxane listens no longer to the words but to the voice; she looks over his shoulder and asks how he can read: "It is too dark to see!"

In the original the two night scenes share the same words. Under the balcony Cyrano excused his faltering: "c'est qu'il fait nuit", "it is because it is night". In the garden Roxane says: "il fait nuit". **The same night that hid him at the start gave him away at the end.** An 18-9-18 couple does not need to escape the Moon. It needs the darkness to stop being a shelter for the image and to become the place where people are recognised by their voice.

Rostand shows the price of silence to the very end. Cyrano denies everything, calling her "my sweet love" in the very sentence in which he swears he never loved her — the endearment tells the truth before the denial is finished. He had forbidden himself tears back in Act I: tenderness seemed ridiculous to him. But his tear remained on the farewell letter, and it is this tear that becomes the evidence. **What he hid as weakness turns out to be the only proof of love.** "I should have guessed, each time he said my name!" says Roxane. She had heard the other voice already under the balcony; what was missing was the question.

The hero had a model, the real Cyrano, and he wrote a novel about a journey to the Moon. It opens with the claim that the Moon is a world like this one, "to which ours serves as a moon". Each partner in such a couple sees the other by the reflected light of their own hopes and fears — and forgets that to the other they are a moon too.
The numbers do not predict the ending of the play: the tail shows a plot, not a fate. Rostand himself left hints at the places where the plot could have turned.

ul: **Believe the permission already given.** Roxane said she would love Christian ugly, even disfigured: "Ay!" Cyrano believed it for a moment and did not get to finish.
**Ask instead of filling in.** Check a guess with words, not with one's own version of the answer, and do not load one's fears onto the partner.
**Say in daylight what is easy to write at night.** One sentence said aloud, face to face, weighs more than a dozen letters.
**Add a line about oneself to the "gazette".** The couple's ritual has room for one piece of news about oneself: "I'm tired", "I'm glad we're together".
**Tell solitude from disappearance.** Withdrawing into oneself is a way to restore strength, not a lack of love, as long as it is said aloud.

report: In the plus this tail is a rare gift: an intuition that recognises a voice in the dark after fifteen years, a shared secret world and a loyalty that needs no witnesses. A strong 18-9-18 couple keeps its night language and adds a daytime one. Its "il fait nuit" means only one thing: time to light the lamp and finish the conversation.
